# Create an R Project {#sec-create-project}

One of the basic steps to reproducibility and modern workflows in data analysis
is to keep everything contained in a single location. In RStudio, this is done
with R Projects.

::: callout-important
If you have not used R Projects before, please read all of the [section on
it](https://r-cubed-intro.rostools.org/sessions/setup-project) from the
introduction workshop to learn about R Projects and how they help keep things
self-contained. *You don't need to do any of the exercises or activities*.
:::

There are several ways to organise a project folder. We'll be using the
structure from the package [prodigenr](https://rostools.github.io/prodigenr/).
The project setup can be done by either:

1. Using RStudio's New Project menu item: "File -\> New Project -\> New
   Directory", scroll down to "Scientific Analysis Project using prodigenr" and
   name the project "AdvancedR3" in the Directory Name, saving it to the
   "Desktop" with Browse. **Note**: You might need to restart RStudio if you
   don't see this option.
2. Or, running the command `prodigenr::setup_project("~/Desktop/AdvancedR3")`
   (or other location like `Documents`) in the R Console and manually switching
   to it using: `File -> Open Project` and navigating to the project location.

```{r}
#| label: purl-only-run-prodigenr
#| echo: false
#| purl: true

prodigenr::setup_project("~/Desktop/AdvancedR3")
usethis::local_project("~/Desktop/AdvancedR3")
```

When the RStudio Project opens up again, run these commands in the R Console to
finish the setup:

```{r}
#| label: more-project-setup
#| filename: Console
#| purl: true

# Create a `functions.R` file in the `R/` folder
usethis::use_r("functions", open = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: purl-only-first-commit
#| echo: false
#| purl: true

git_ci(".", "First commit.")
```

Here we use the `{usethis}` package to help set things up. `{usethis}` is an
extremely useful package for managing R Projects and we highly recommend
checking it out more to see how you can use it in your own work.

Since we will be using Git a lot for this workshop, do a quick check to make
sure your Git is connected to the project and to RStudio. You should see the Git
tab in one of the panes in RStudio or the Git icon beside the "Go to" search bar
below the menu bar of RStudio. If you don't see it, try [these
troubleshooting](https://happygitwithr.com/troubleshooting) steps.

## R Markdown and Quarto

We teach and use R Markdown/Quarto because it is one of the very first steps to
being reproducible and because it is a very powerful tool to doing data
analysis. You may or may not have heard of or used either R Markdown or Quarto.

Quarto is a next generation version of R Markdown and comes bundled with
RStudio. Quarto, like R Markdown, is a way of writing text and code together to
create reproducible documents of analyses. Quarto uses Markdown syntax and
allows you to create many types of output documents (like books, websites,
slides). There are many options for customizing these outputs.

::: callout-important
If you have *not* used Quarto or R Markdown before, please read over the [Quarto
section](https://r-cubed-intro.rostools.org/sessions/reproducible-documents.html)
of the introduction workshop. *Don't do the exercises*.
:::

While inside the `AdvancedR3` project, run this function in the R Console to
create a new Quarto file called `learning.qmd` in the `docs/` folder.

```{r}
#| label: add-rmarkdown-doc
#| filename: Console
#| purl: true

r3::create_learning_qmd()
```

```{r}
#| label: purl-only-add-lesson-rmd
#| echo: false
#| purl: true

git_ci("docs/learning.qmd", "Add draft lesson qmd file.")
```
